concept: verb inflectional forms
statement: Most verbs have six inflectional forms: three primary (preterite, 3rd singular present, plain present) and three secondary (plain form, gerund-participle, past participle).
condition: Applies to the inflectional paradigm of an ordinary (non-be) verb lexeme: primary forms are preterite, 3rd person singular present tense and plain present tense; secondary forms are the plain form, the gerund-participle and the past participle.

He writes it. [3rd sg present]
They write it. [plain present]
I need to write it. [plain form]
We are writing it. [gerund-participle]
They have written it. [past participle]
The stones had been trodden smooth by visitors. [past participle related to the preterite trod]

concept: case forms of pronouns and nouns
statement: A few pronouns have four case forms (we, us, our, ours); most nouns contrast only genitive and plain case, case is determined by the NP's function, and genitive is marked on the last word of the NP (head genitive or phrasal genitive).

concept: negative forms of lexical verbs
statement: Auxiliaries have additional negative primary forms, whereas lexical verbs do not have corresponding negative inflectional forms.

concept: inflectional paradigm of prototypical nouns
statement: Prototypical nouns distinguish singular and plural number and plain and genitive case, yielding singular plain, singular genitive, plural plain, and plural genitive forms.
condition: For a prototypical noun lexeme with both singular and plural forms, the paradigm crosses the number distinction (singular/plural) with the case distinction (plain/genitive).

concept: lexical base distinguished from inflectional forms
statement: A lexical base is the reference form from which the inflectional paradigm is described; it is distinct from any individual inflectional form even though one or more inflected forms often coincide with the base.
condition: For a variable lexeme, identify its lexical base separately from its attested singular, plural or other inflectional forms; a defective lexeme can have a base for which no corresponding independent form exists, and several forms can coincide with the base.

exceptions.description: Defective lexemes may lack a surface form corresponding to the lexical base; several inflectional forms can also be identical to the lexical base.

contrast.text: The dregs settled at the bottom. [plural-only noun, with a lexical base dreg- not used as a plain singular form]
One sheep escaped through the fence. [singular coincides with the lexical base]
Several sheep escaped through the fence. [plural also coincides with the same lexical base]
A worker greeted the visitors. [the singular matches the lexical base of worker]

concept: inflection of simple and complex lexical bases
statement: In English, a lexeme's base can be internally simple or morphologically complex, and regular inflectional operations generally apply to either kind without changing their basic formation rules.
condition: When a noun's lexical base is simple (e.g., dog) or consists of morphological units (e.g., worker), apply the ordinary plural suffixation operation to the complete lexical base, rather than treating internal derivational complexity as a reason for a different plural rule.

contrast.text: Two dogs waited outside the office. [simple base dog, regular plural]
Two workers waited outside the office. [complex base worker, regular plural]
The trainer hired three workers. [inflection attaches to the whole complex lexical base]

concept: morphological operations in English inflection
statement: English inflection can use suffixation, change to a lexical base such as vowel alternation, or a combination of a suffix and a modified base.
condition: When describing the formation of a noun or verb inflectional form, distinguish a suffix added to an unchanged base from internal vowel replacement and from the combined use of suffixation and a modified base.

concept: multi-step inflection from an already inflected form
statement: Most English inflectional forms coincide with or are formed directly from the lexical base, but some forms are produced by an additional operation on another inflectional form.
condition: When analysing the genitive plural of a noun such as child, attach the genitive suffix to its plural rather than to the singular base; for the small set of past participles exemplified by trodden, identify the preterite trod as the input to a further -en suffixation.

concept: morphological alternation
statement: Morphological alternation occurs when the same morphological unit has different surface realisations depending on its context, such as the written plural suffix variants -s and -es.

concept: regular versus irregular inflection
statement: An inflectional form is regular if its formation follows a lexeme-independent general rule, but irregular if the lexeme requires specific stored information about that form or one of its components.
condition: When classifying plural, preterite or participial forms, check whether their formation follows productive formation rules without lexical exceptions; where the resulting form must be separately specified for a particular lexeme, classify it as irregular even if it also contains an ordinary affix.

concept: syncretism of inflectional forms
statement: Syncretism is identity of pronunciation or spelling between two or more distinct inflectional forms of the same lexeme.

concept: established words
statement: An established word is recognised by speakers as an individual vocabulary item; it can have an idiosyncratic or historically inherited formation that need not be available for making new words.
condition: Classify a lexical item as established when it is conventionally familiar in the language, rather than merely matching a productive construction; an established form can remain usable even when the process that first produced it has ceased to be productive.

concept: potential words
statement: A potential word is a non-established word whose formation accords with Present-day English word-formation rules, whether or not anyone has previously used it.
condition: For a proposed lexical word that is not already part of the established vocabulary, classify it as potential if it is morphologically admissible under an available word-formation process, without requiring prior attestation or a dictionary entry.

statement: A nonce-word has been used on an occasion but has not become established, while the larger class of potential words also includes well-formed coinages that have never been used.

concept: productive layered verb-to-adjective-to-noun formation
statement: A verb can form an adjective with the productive suffix -able, and that adjective can form a noun with -ity, with a change in the ending, to express a property of the original action.
condition: For a verb that licenses -able, analyse a derived nominal such as repairability as an adjective stage in -able followed by noun-forming -ity, taking account of the -able to -ability shape; do not assume every verb must allow this derivation.

exceptions.description: The two-step pattern is available only where the verb supports the adjective-forming -able derivation; the subsection does not license it indiscriminately for all verbs.

concept: Clause finiteness is a syntactic category
statement: English finiteness is classified at clause level: primary verbs, imperative and subjunctive plain forms occur in finite clauses, whereas infinitivals and participials are non-finite.
condition: Apply to full clause constructions rather than assigning a finite/non-finite feature solely from the surface form of a verb.

correct.text: Close the door. [finite imperative]
She requires that he close the door. [finite subjunctive]
To close the door would help. [non-finite infinitival]

concept: Negative imperative differs from negative infinitival
statement: Imperative clauses can use auxiliary don't for negation, but negative infinitival clauses take not and cannot use do-support in the same position.
condition: Apply to a negative infinitival clause introduced by infinitival to with a directly following auxiliary don't/do not construction.
violation: Attempting imperative do-support after infinitival to in an otherwise infinitival subordinate clause.

exceptions.description: Do-support belongs to the negative imperative, which is a finite clause, not to the infinitival use of the plain form.

correct.text: She asked me not to leave.
Don't leave before dinner.

incorrect.text: She asked me to don't leave.
He wanted to don't interrupt the meeting.

concept: Finite status of imperative and subjunctive clauses
statement: Imperatives normally behave as finite main clauses, and subjunctives are finite despite their plain verb form and usual subordination.
condition: Apply when distinguishing plain-form imperative and subjunctive constructions from non-finite infinitivals.

correct.text: Don't shout during the lecture. [imperative]
The chair requested that she attend. [subjunctive]

concept: Infinitival subjects and subordinator for
statement: Non-finite infinitivals generally lack an overt subject; where one occurs, it is introduced by for and personal pronouns appear in accusative case.
condition: Apply to overt-subject to-infinitival subordinate clauses as contrasted with tensed declarative that-clauses.

correct.text: It would be unusual for him to arrive late.
It is strange that he arrives late.

concept: Negative inflection contrasted with subject cliticisation
statement: Negative auxiliaries such as won't are inflectional verb forms, whereas subject-attached reductions such as 'll are clitics and belong to two-word sequences syntactically.
condition: Use the distinction when analysing negation on an auxiliary versus phonological reduction of an auxiliary onto a neighbouring host.

correct.text: Tara won't attend. [negative auxiliary form]
Tara'll attend. [subject plus auxiliary clitic]

concept: Plain negative don't in imperative clauses
statement: The plain negative form don't in an imperative is unaffected by a third-person singular subject, unlike present-tense doesn't in questions.
condition: Distinguish an imperative with an overt third-person subject from a present-tense interrogative when classifying negative auxiliary do.

correct.text: Don't anyone move the chairs! [imperative]
Doesn't anybody remember the route? [present-tense question]

concept: Modal preterites and modal remoteness
statement: Preterite modal forms such as could and would can signal modal remoteness in a main clause instead of past time.
condition: The first verb of an independent clause is a modal preterite used for a hypothetical or polite non-past interpretation.

correct.text: Could you assist with the display? [polite request]
They might arrive this evening. [non-past possibility]

concept: Defective preterite paradigms of must and ought
statement: Contemporary must and ought have no separate preterite inflectional forms.
condition: The lexeme must or ought is classified in a context where a distinct present-versus-preterite inflectional opposition would otherwise be expected.

correct.text: The applicant must submit the form today.
The coordinator ought to explain the arrangement.

concept: Secondary forms of perfect auxiliary have
statement: Perfect auxiliary have can appear in plain and gerund-participle forms, but has no past-participle form within the perfect auxiliary paradigm.
condition: Perfect have heads the perfect construction and is inflected inside modal or non-finite contexts.

correct.text: They might have finished already.
Having finished early, she closed the office.

concept: Idiosyncratic preterite uses of should
statement: Some deontic uses of should have a meaning not compositionally derived from present-tense shall plus ordinary preterite remoteness.
condition: Should expresses advice or an evaluation in a clause where a corresponding shall construction does not preserve the meaning.

correct.text: You should bring your notes tomorrow.
She should read the instructions first.

concept: Possible lexical split between may and might
statement: For some speakers may and might may function as separate modal lexemes instead of a present–preterite inflectional pair.
condition: Compare modal may and might in a variety whose time and remoteness uses no longer align as a single lexeme.

correct.text: The gallery may reopen tomorrow.
The gallery might reopen tomorrow.

concept: Defective inflectional paradigm of aspectual use
statement: Aspectual use expressing former habit is largely restricted to a preterite and to a plain form after supportive do, without an ordinary present or -ing paradigm.
condition: A use lexeme conveys past habitual aspect, not the unrelated lexical verb use meaning employ.

correct.text: They used to gather before noon.
They did not use to gather before noon.
